facts.text: The white-throated gerygone lives in Australia and Papua New Guinea.
facts.quote: It is found in Australia and Papua New Guinea.

facts.text: It makes its home in temperate forests and subtropical or tropical moist lowland forests.
facts.quote: Its natural habitats are temperate forests and subtropical or tropical moist lowland forests.

facts.text: The white-throated gerygone also goes by the names white-throated warbler, white-throated flyeater, bush canary, and native canary.
facts.quote: Its common names include white-throated warbler, white-throated flyeater, bush canary, and native canary.

facts.text: It favours open dry eucalyptus woodland and dense riparian vegetation.
facts.quote: The white-throated gerygone is primarily found in open dry eucalyptus woodland and dense riparian vegetation.

facts.text: The white-throated gerygone lives in tropical, subtropical, and temperate zones.
facts.quote: It occupies tropical, subtropical, and temperate zones.

facts.text: It sometimes turns up in remnant woods on farmland, in gardens, and in open eucalypt savannah.
facts.quote: Less commonly, it may occur in remnant woods in farmland and gardens, and in open eucalypt savannah.

facts.text: In New Guinea it can be found in Melaleuca, or paperbark, forests from the coast up to 650 m.
facts.quote: In New Guinea, they may be found in Melaleuca (paperbark) forests from the coast to 650 m.

facts.text: The genus name Gerygone comes from the Greek word 'gerugonos', meaning 'echos'.
facts.quote: Gerygone comes from the Greek word "gerugonos" meaning "echos".

facts.text: The species name olivacea is Latin for 'olive-green', a nod to its underbelly colour.
facts.quote: The species name olivacea is latin for 'olive-green', given for its underbelly coloration.
